title: The Breath That Took a Journey

pages.text: The Breath That Took a Journey A story about the respiratory system

“Oxygen?” Lucas asked. Ms. Bennett smiled. “Oxygen is a gas in the air your body needs it to make energy.” Saanvi touched her nose. “So the air starts here?” “Yes,” said Ms. Bennett. “Air can enter through your nose or mouth. Your nose is especially helpful because it warms, moistens, and filters the air.” Lucas sniffed. “So my nose is like air cleaner?” “Exactly,” said Ms. Bennett. “After air enters, it travels down a tube called the trachea, or windpipe.” Nia and Ben raced across the playground until they were puffing and laughing. “Why am I breathing so fast?” Nia asked. Back in class, Ms. Alvarez smiled. “Let’s follow one breath and find out.” She explained that air usually enters through the nose, where tiny hairs and mucus help trap dust. Air can also enter through the mouth. From there, the breath passes down the throat and into the trachea, a strong tube that carries air toward the lungs.

Inside the chest, the trachea splits into two large tubes called the bronchi, one leading to each lung. The bronchi divide again and again into smaller tubes called bronchioles, almost like the branches of a tree. These tiny pathways guide air deep into the lungs. Ben pictured his breath traveling through a hidden tunnel map, branching farther and farther with every inhale.

At the ends of the tiniest bronchioles are millions of tiny air sacs called alveoli. This is where the most important trade happens. Oxygen from the air moves from the alveoli into the blood. At the same time, carbon dioxide, a waste gas the body does not need, moves from the blood into the alveoli so it can be breathed out. “So every breath is a delivery and a cleanup!” Ben whispered.

“But what helps the lungs move?” asked Nia. Ms. Alvarez pointed to a broad muscle under the lungs called the diaphragm. When the diaphragm moves downward, the lungs expand and fill with air. When it relaxes and moves upward, air is pushed back out. She also reminded the class that the rib cage protects the lungs while they do their important work.

Soon the class could name the whole path of a breath: nose or mouth → throat → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli. “The respiratory system works with the blood and the heart to help every body part get oxygen,” said Ms. Alvarez. “That is why breathing matters when you run, sleep, sing, or even sit quietly reading.” Nia smiled. “A breath seems simple,” she said, “but it travels a very important road.”

Saari and Lucas were running across the playground during P.E. Lucas stopped near the finish line and put his hands on his knees. "I'm breathing so fast!" he said. Saari took a deep breath. "Me too. It feels like my body is asking for more air." Their teacher, Mr. Bennett, smiled. "That is exactly what is happening," she said. "When you run, your muscles need more oxygen."
